WHERE IT SITS. The statutory counterpart to the sector's own reporting, published by the licensing authority. WHY IT MATTERS. A large share of procedures are for the breeding and maintenance of genetically altered animals rather than for experiments on them — animals created and killed to sustain a line. That distinction appears in these statistics and almost nowhere else, and it is the clearest available measure of what the model-organism trade actually costs.

name: Federal Research Center for Animal Husbandry
desc: WHAT. Russia's principal livestock research institute, working on gene-edited cattle and the national livestock gene pool. WHERE IT SITS. Inside a country that banned GM crop cultivation in 2016 while continuing state-funded genetic research. WHY IT MATTERS. Prohibition on cultivation and heavy investment in the underlying science are not contradictory positions; they are a state deciding it wants the capability without the imports. Any account of this industry that treats a cultivation ban as the end of the story misses where the research actually continues.

name: Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry — biosafety board
desc: WHAT. Turkey's competent authority, which permits GM feed imports under an approved-event list while prohibiting GM cultivation entirely, with criminal penalties attached. WHERE IT SITS. A large importer with a hard cultivation ban — an uncommon combination. WHY IT MATTERS. Turkey demonstrates that a country can refuse to grow engineered crops while importing them at volume, which is the arrangement most cultivation bans actually amount to. The ban is real, the exposure continues, and the difference between those two facts is where most public argument about bans goes wrong.

name: Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food
desc: WHAT. Ukraine's agriculture ministry, overseeing one of the world's largest grain and oilseed export sectors. WHERE IT SITS. A major exporter whose crop moves into markets with sharply different GM rules. WHY IT MATTERS. Ukrainian grain reaches importers that require GM-free certification and importers that do not care, which makes its own domestic position commercially consequential well beyond its borders. Unapproved GM soy has been documented growing in Ukraine for years despite cultivation not being authorised, which puts it alongside India and Brazil in the pattern of adoption preceding approval.

name: PT Perkebunan Nusantara / sugarcane biotechnology
desc: WHAT. Indonesia's state plantation group, involved in the deployment of domestically developed drought-tolerant engineered sugarcane. WHERE IT SITS. State-owned plantation agriculture using nationally developed traits rather than licensed multinational ones. WHY IT MATTERS. Indonesia approved engineered sugarcane developed by its own institutions, which is an unusual route: most countries either import traits or import the argument. A domestically owned trait deployed through a state plantation company answers to a different set of pressures than a licensed one, and produces a different politics.

name: Ministry of Agriculture and Environment — biosafety
desc: WHAT. Viet Nam's competent authority, which has authorised GM maize for cultivation and imports feed grain at large volume. WHERE IT SITS. One of the few Southeast Asian countries to approve cultivation rather than import only. WHY IT MATTERS. Mekong-region seed moves across borders informally at scale, so an approval in one country becomes a practical fact in several. National frameworks in this region are partly notional for that reason, and understanding them as such is more useful than reading them as boundaries.

name: ICA — Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario
desc: WHAT. Colombia's agricultural authority, handling GM crop authorisations and the seed registration rules that go with them. WHERE IT SITS. At the southern edge of maize diversity, in a country whose seed-certification rules triggered mass farmer protest. WHY IT MATTERS. Colombia's attempt to restrict the sale of uncertified seed produced nationwide strikes and was suspended. It is the clearest case in the Americas of seed law — not biosafety law — being the thing that mobilised people, which is worth noting because seed law is where most of this industry's control actually sits.

name: SLU — Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences
desc: WHAT. Sweden's agricultural university, running gene-editing research on crops and forest trees and advising on regulatory classification. WHERE IT SITS. Where public research meets the European argument about whether edited organisms should be regulated at all. WHY IT MATTERS. Public universities have been among the most active advocates for treating edited crops as conventional, on the grounds that the alternative locks small public breeders out. That is a real argument and it is also the argument the largest companies benefit from most, which is worth holding both halves of.

name: Solar Foods
desc: WHAT. A Finnish company producing a protein from a microbe grown on carbon dioxide, hydrogen and electricity rather than on agricultural feedstock. WHERE IT SITS. The far edge of fermentation — food production decoupled from farmland altogether. WHY IT MATTERS. If protein can be made from air and electricity, the land argument that underpins most defences of engineered agriculture weakens considerably. It also concentrates food production into industrial facilities owned by whoever built them, which is a different distribution of control from farming, not obviously a better one.

name: Teagasc
desc: WHAT. Ireland's agriculture and food development authority, running research on crops, dairy genetics and livestock breeding. WHERE IT SITS. A public body combining research, extension and advisory work in a country positioning its agriculture as GM-free for market reasons. WHY IT MATTERS. Ireland's dairy and beef export brand depends on a pasture-fed image, which makes GM feed a commercial question before it is an environmental one. That is the same reasoning Tasmania uses, and it works: a market-access argument is harder for the industry to answer than a safety one.

name: Cyagen
desc: WHAT. A contract company generating custom transgenic and knockout animal models to client specification, operating across the United States and China. WHERE IT SITS. Custom model generation — the made-to-order end of the animal trade. WHY IT MATTERS. A researcher can now commission an animal that does not yet exist, engineered to a written specification, delivered as a product with a lead time. The organism is the deliverable. There is no register of these animals because contained use rarely generates one, so the largest volume of vertebrate engineering in the world is also the least recorded.

name: National Primate Research Centers
desc: WHAT. The federally supported network of primate research centres in the United States, breeding and supplying non-human primates including genetically modified lines. WHERE IT SITS. The most ethically contested corner of the animal facet, and one of the least visible. WHY IT MATTERS. Primate supply is a chronic constraint on this kind of research, and demand has driven both domestic breeding expansion and international trade in wild-caught animals, with associated smuggling prosecutions. The scarcity is what makes the trade lucrative and the enforcement problems predictable.

name: Bachem
desc: WHAT. A Swiss manufacturer of peptides and oligonucleotides at commercial scale, supplying pharmaceutical companies worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. The manufacturing bottleneck for oligonucleotide therapeutics, a class of medicine that depends entirely on synthesis capacity. WHY IT MATTERS. Oligonucleotide drugs are designed on a computer and made in a factory, which sounds like it should make them cheap. They are not, because a handful of plants can make them at the required purity. Manufacturing scarcity, not science, sets the price for a growing share of genetic medicine.

name: Samsung Biologics
desc: WHAT. One of the world's largest contract manufacturers of biologics, with very large-scale capacity in Songdo. WHERE IT SITS. The manufacturing layer for antibodies and engineered proteins, serving clients who own the products. WHY IT MATTERS. Biologics manufacturing capacity is concentrated in a handful of sites globally, and a single company's allocation decisions determine which therapies reach market and when. That is commercial scheduling deciding a clinical outcome, and it happens entirely outside any regulator's view.

name: Virtus Health
desc: WHAT. A large fertility clinic group operating across Australia, Ireland, Denmark, Singapore and the UK, taken private by an investment firm. WHERE IT SITS. The consolidation pattern arriving in a country with strong clinic regulation. WHY IT MATTERS. Australia regulates fertility clinics comparatively well, and the ownership still consolidated into private equity hands operating across five countries. Clinic-level regulation does not reach the ownership layer, which is where pricing, add-on services and expansion decisions are actually taken.

name: Israeli fertility system — Ministry of Health
desc: WHAT. The regulator of a fertility system with the highest per-capita IVF utilisation in the world, largely state-funded and effectively unlimited for eligible patients. WHERE IT SITS. The opposite pole from the American arrangement: publicly funded, heavily used, closely regulated. WHY IT MATTERS. It shows what happens when cost is removed as a constraint on assisted reproduction — utilisation rises very high, and the ethical questions about selection and embryo disposition arrive at population scale rather than for the wealthy few. Neither the American nor the Israeli arrangement resolves those questions; they just meet them from opposite directions.

name: Predator Free 2050 — genetic tools debate
desc: WHAT. New Zealand's national programme to eradicate introduced predators, within which the use of gene drives and other genetic tools has been formally debated and, so far, not adopted. WHERE IT SITS. The most advanced national conversation anywhere about whether to use a gene drive on a conservation problem. WHY IT MATTERS. New Zealand has a strong case for genetic predator control, a capable research base, and has still not authorised it — partly because Māori consultation raised questions the programme could not answer about who decides for a species. That is a country taking the consent question seriously enough to slow itself down, which is rare enough to be worth marking.

name: Sovereign wealth investment in agrifood technology
desc: WHAT. Gulf sovereign wealth funds investing heavily in agricultural technology, vertical farming, cultivated protein and seed businesses. WHERE IT SITS. State capital from food-importing countries buying into the technology that might reduce their import dependence. WHY IT MATTERS. Sovereign funds have no exit deadline, which removes the pressure that shapes venture-backed companies, and no electorate in the countries where they invest. It is a materially different kind of money entering this industry, and it is growing while the venture cycle contracts.

name: National Biosafety Centre — Ministry of Climate Change
desc: WHAT. Pakistan's biosafety authority, overseeing a cotton sector in which Bt varieties dominate almost entirely. WHERE IT SITS. One of the world's largest cotton producers, where the trait arrived through unlicensed channels before any framework was ready. WHY IT MATTERS. Pakistani Bt cotton spread through informal seed multiplication rather than through licensed sale, which means the traits in the field are unlicensed copies of varying quality. Yields have fallen and pest resistance has risen. It is the clearest demonstration that a trait without a functioning seed system behind it degrades rather than persists.

name: Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute — Bt brinjal
desc: WHAT. The public institute that developed and released Bt brinjal, the first engineered food crop grown commercially in South Asia, using a trait donated by Mahyco. WHERE IT SITS. A public breeding programme deploying a corporate trait, supported by foreign development funding. WHY IT MATTERS. This is the model the industry now prefers in low-income countries: the trait is donated, the public institute carries the approval and the public reputation, and the company carries neither the cost nor the blame. Whatever the outcome for farmers, the arrangement moves the accountability away from whoever built the trait.

name: Ethiopian Environment Protection Authority — biosafety
desc: WHAT. Ethiopia's biosafety authority, which administers a framework substantially loosened in 2015 after an earlier and unusually strict law. WHERE IT SITS. A centre of origin for coffee, sorghum, teff and enset, with one of Africa's oldest genebanks. WHY IT MATTERS. Ethiopia wrote one of the strictest biosafety laws in the world, including strict liability and criminal penalties, and then amended it under sustained pressure to permit confined trials. The sequence is worth knowing: the strict law was achievable, and it was reversed by the same channels that write the loose ones.

name: National Biosafety Authority Ghana
desc: WHAT. Ghana's permit authority, which approved Bt cowpea for commercial release, making Ghana one of the first African countries to grow an engineered food crop. WHERE IT SITS. West Africa's second commercial approval after Nigeria, in the same crop. WHY IT MATTERS. Ghana's Plant Variety Protection Act carries a minimum ten-year prison term for infringing breeders' rights. Approval of an engineered crop and criminal enforcement of seed ownership arrived through the same legislative period, from the same advisory sources. The two are usually discussed separately; here they are one process.

name: Gabinete Nacional de Bioseguridad
desc: WHAT. Uruguay's biosafety cabinet, authorising GM soy and maize cultivation in a country whose agriculture is overwhelmingly export-facing. WHERE IT SITS. A small producer whose entire commercial logic is set by what its buyers accept. WHY IT MATTERS. Uruguay also runs one of the world's most complete livestock traceability systems, tracking individual cattle from birth to slaughter. A country that can trace every animal cannot claim traceability of engineered crops is technically impossible. The capability exists there; it is simply not applied to seed.

name: SENAVE — seed and plant health service
desc: WHAT. Paraguay's seed and plant health authority, regulating seed registration and GM approvals in a major soy exporter. WHERE IT SITS. A country where engineered soy arrived through unauthorised cross-border planting from Brazil years before approval. WHY IT MATTERS. Paraguay is the third case on this map of adoption preceding approval, after India and Brazil. In each the regulator's eventual decision was whether to legalise what was already there. That is not an assessment; it is a ratification, and it is how a large share of the world's engineered crop area actually arrived.

name: SAG — Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero
desc: WHAT. Chile's agricultural service, authorising GM seed multiplication for export while prohibiting domestic commercial cultivation. WHERE IT SITS. The counter-season multiplication hub for the northern hemisphere seed industry — engineered seed is grown in Chile and shipped out. WHY IT MATTERS. Chile grows engineered crops that Chileans may not plant. The site locations were withheld as commercial confidence until the transparency council ordered otherwise. A country hosting the industry's off-season production while barring its own farmers from the same seed is an arrangement worth naming plainly.

name: Ministerio de Agricultura — GM cultivation register
desc: WHAT. Spain's agriculture ministry, publishing the annual area of MON 810 maize by province — essentially the whole of EU GM cultivation. WHERE IT SITS. The single member state where European GM cultivation actually happens, concentrated in Aragón and Cataluña. WHY IT MATTERS. European debate about GM crops proceeds largely as though cultivation were hypothetical. It is not; it is happening in two Spanish provinces and has been for two decades. The coexistence rules, the contamination disputes and the organic sector's losses are all documented there rather than in the abstract.

name: Direção-Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária
desc: WHAT. Portugal's authority for GM crop notification, running the EU's mandatory register of who is planting engineered maize and where, parcel by parcel. WHERE IT SITS. The other EU member state with commercial GM cultivation, at much smaller scale than Spain. WHY IT MATTERS. Portugal requires growers to notify their parcels and publishes the register, which is the coexistence transparency Spain does not match. Two neighbouring countries under the same EU framework, with materially different public visibility — which shows the difference is a national choice rather than a legal constraint.

name: Ministry of Agriculture — biotechnology
desc: WHAT. Romania's agriculture ministry, overseeing a sector that grew engineered soy at scale before EU accession and has argued for its return ever since. WHERE IT SITS. The clearest case of accession removing a crop a country was already growing. WHY IT MATTERS. Romania planted herbicide-tolerant soy widely until joining the EU in 2007 required it to stop. Farmers' organisations have pressed for reauthorisation since. It is the one European case where the counterfactual is not hypothetical: the country grew it, stopped, and can compare.

name: Agricultural Genetic Engineering Research Institute
desc: WHAT. Egypt's national agricultural biotechnology institute, developing engineered crops domestically since the 1990s. WHERE IT SITS. A long-standing public research programme in the world's largest wheat importer. WHY IT MATTERS. Egypt developed engineered maize and had it briefly in commercial cultivation before withdrawal, and continues research without commercial release. A country can maintain full technical capability for decades and still not deploy — which separates the capability question from the deployment question that public argument usually conflates.

name: Nuseed / Nufarm omega-3 canola
desc: WHAT. An engineered canola producing long-chain omega-3 oils normally obtained from fish, grown under contract in Canada and the United States for aquaculture feed. WHERE IT SITS. Where an engineered land crop substitutes for a marine input. WHY IT MATTERS. The product exists because industrial aquaculture consumes wild-caught fish for feed faster than the fisheries can supply it. The engineering answers a problem created by another industrial system rather than by agriculture, which is increasingly the pattern across this whole map.

name: Health Canada — novel food decisions
desc: WHAT. The published decisions on novel foods, including foods from gene-edited plants that Canada does not require to be notified at all. WHERE IT SITS. The food-safety half of the trait-based system, separate from the environmental decision. WHY IT MATTERS. Canada requires no pre-market notification for many gene-edited foods judged equivalent to conventional ones, relying instead on a voluntary transparency database maintained by the seed industry. The public record of what is being eaten is therefore kept by the sector that produces it.

name: Aldevron (Danaher)
desc: WHAT. A large manufacturer of plasmid DNA, mRNA and proteins used as raw materials in gene therapy, vaccines and cell engineering. WHERE IT SITS. Upstream of the clinical facet — the material that therapies are built from, made to order at scale. WHY IT MATTERS. Two of the largest suppliers of genetic raw materials, this and IDT, sit inside the same conglomerate. That concentration is invisible from either company's name, and it means decisions about who may buy the building blocks of engineered biology are taken at one corporate level answerable to no biosafety authority.

name: Pacific Biosciences
desc: WHAT. Maker of long-read sequencing instruments, used where short-read platforms cannot resolve complex or repetitive genome regions. WHERE IT SITS. The technical complement to Illumina rather than a competitor at scale. WHY IT MATTERS. Long-read sequencing is what makes it possible to verify whether an edit went where it was supposed to and whether anything else came with it. The verification capability exists and is commercially available; whether a developer uses it before release is generally their own decision.

name: Bio-Rad Laboratories
desc: WHAT. Supplier of the detection instruments and reagents used to test for genetically modified material in food, feed and seed. WHERE IT SITS. The testing layer — what a regulator, an importer or a certifier uses to find out what is in a shipment. WHY IT MATTERS. Detection depends on knowing what to look for. Event-specific tests exist for approved transgenic events and generally not for gene-edited organisms, which carry no inserted sequence to target. The instruments are capable; the reference material is what is missing, and that is a consequence of deregulation rather than of chemistry.

name: Intellia Therapeutics
desc: WHAT. A gene-editing company running the first clinical trials of CRISPR delivered in vivo — edited inside the patient's body rather than in cells removed and returned. WHERE IT SITS. The step past ex-vivo therapy, and the point at which an edit stops being confined to a treated cell population. WHY IT MATTERS. An in-vivo edit cannot be recalled from the patient any more than a released organism can be recalled from a field. It is somatic, so it is not inherited, but the irreversibility argument this map makes about the environment applies to a body as well, and it applies first to the people in early trials.

name: Sarepta Therapeutics
desc: WHAT. Developer of gene therapies and antisense drugs for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, several approved on accelerated pathways against contested evidence. WHERE IT SITS. The regulatory frontier of genetic medicine — approvals granted on surrogate markers rather than demonstrated clinical benefit. WHY IT MATTERS. Accelerated approval trades certainty for speed, on the argument that a fatal disease cannot wait. Sarepta's approvals have been granted over the objections of the agency's own reviewers more than once. Whether that is courage or capture depends on the case, and the documents in both directions are public.

name: FDA — cellular & gene therapy approvals
desc: WHAT. The register of approved cell and gene therapy products in the United States, with the review documents behind each. WHERE IT SITS. The public record for the clinical facet, and the closest analogue to a release register for human genetic engineering. WHY IT MATTERS. The review packages include the reviewers' own dissents where they exist. As with Brazil's CTNBio opinions, the internal disagreement inside an approval is more informative than the decision, and it is published.

name: Alliance for Regenerative Medicine
desc: WHAT. The trade association for the cell and gene therapy sector, publishing sector data and lobbying on reimbursement, regulation and manufacturing policy. WHERE IT SITS. The clinical facet's collective voice, doing for gene therapy what BIO does for agricultural biotechnology. WHY IT MATTERS. Its sector reports are the standard source for trial counts and financing figures, quoted widely including by critics. Useful data from an interested party, which is the ordinary condition of information in this field rather than an exception.

name: Flagship Pioneering
desc: WHAT. A venture firm that creates companies rather than funding existing ones, originating businesses across agriculture, synthetic biology and therapeutics, including Moderna and Inari. WHERE IT SITS. Earlier than venture capital usually sits — the company exists because the fund decided the idea should. WHY IT MATTERS. When a fund originates the company, the commercial thesis precedes the science rather than following it. That is the clearest available answer to why this industry builds what it builds: the target is chosen for its market before anyone works out whether it is a good idea.

name: USDA NIFA — grant database
desc: WHAT. The searchable record of US agricultural research grants, with recipient, amount, project description and commercial partners. WHERE IT SITS. Public money in agricultural biotechnology, published in full. WHY IT MATTERS. It answers the question the industry's own materials avoid: how much of this was paid for publicly. The grant record shows public funds, a university, and a commercial partner on the same project, with the licence terms decided separately and rarely published. That gap between what the public paid for and what it owns is documented here rather than alleged.

name: Verily — Debug programme
desc: WHAT. Alphabet's life-sciences arm, which ran large-scale releases of Wolbachia-infected sterile male mosquitoes with automated rearing and release systems. WHERE IT SITS. A technology company entering open release, with engineering capacity no biology institute has. WHY IT MATTERS. Automated mass rearing changes the scale question. When releasing tens of millions of insects becomes an engineering problem rather than a biological one, the constraint on how much gets released stops being capacity and becomes only permission — which puts far more weight on the permission than the systems granting it were built for.

name: Greenlight Biosciences
desc: WHAT. A company producing RNA-based pesticides, including a double-stranded RNA product for Colorado potato beetle registered in the United States. WHERE IT SITS. A new category: not an engineered organism but engineered genetic material sprayed onto crops to silence a gene in the pest. WHY IT MATTERS. RNA pesticides fall outside GMO frameworks because nothing living is modified, and outside conventional pesticide assumptions because the mechanism is sequence-specific. The regulatory category was built for neither, and the product is on the market while the category is still being argued about.

name: Genomics England
desc: WHAT. The government-owned company that sequenced 100,000 genomes from NHS patients and now runs the national genomic dataset, including a newborn sequencing programme. WHERE IT SITS. Where public health data becomes a research asset that industry pays to access. WHY IT MATTERS. Participants consented to research use; the commercial access arrangements built on top were designed afterwards. Sequencing newborns raises the question this map keeps returning to in another form — a person whose genome is read before they can be asked, in a dataset that will outlive the consent framework that gathered it.

name: Roche / Genentech
desc: WHAT. One of the largest biotechnology companies in the world, producing recombinant therapeutic proteins and antibodies at industrial scale, and owner of a major diagnostics business. WHERE IT SITS. The commercial mainstream of genetic engineering applied to medicine — the part that has been ordinary for forty years. WHY IT MATTERS. Genentech made the first recombinant human insulin, which is where medical and agricultural biotechnology parted company in the public mind. The same technique, applied to a drug, became uncontroversial; applied to a crop, it did not. That divergence is about who benefits and who was asked, not about the science.

name: Leaps by Bayer
desc: WHAT. Bayer's venture arm, investing in early-stage companies across agriculture, cell and gene therapy, and reproductive health, separately from the operating businesses. WHERE IT SITS. A major incumbent buying options on the technologies that might displace it. WHY IT MATTERS. Corporate venture money means a company that dominates one part of this industry holds positions across the parts that could disrupt it — including reproductive health, which most accounts of agricultural biotechnology never connect to a seed company. The facets on this map are more joined up at the ownership level than at any other.

name: Oxitec do Brasil
desc: WHAT. Oxitec's Brazilian operation, which has run the largest and longest sustained releases of engineered mosquitoes anywhere, with a dedicated production facility. WHERE IT SITS. The country where engineered insect release moved from trial to routine deployment. WHY IT MATTERS. Brazil approved unrestricted commercial release of engineered Aedes, which no other country has. Everything known about what happens when engineered insects are released continuously over years — including the Jacobina introgression finding — comes from Brazilian releases, because nowhere else has run them long enough.

name: WuXi Biologics Ireland
desc: WHAT. A large biologics manufacturing campus in Dundalk, part of the WuXi Biologics network, serving European and American clients. WHERE IT SITS. Manufacturing capacity built in Europe by a Chinese group, for Western pharmaceutical companies. WHY IT MATTERS. Attempts to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing capacity run into the fact that a good deal of the European capacity is owned by the same groups. Ownership and location are different questions, and policy arguments about this industry routinely conflate them.

name: Lonza Singapore / biologics cluster
desc: WHAT. Singapore's state-assembled biologics manufacturing cluster, built through investment incentives and hosting several of the largest contract manufacturers. WHERE IT SITS. A country that chose to become manufacturing infrastructure for this industry as national policy. WHY IT MATTERS. Capacity does not appear where the science is; it appears where a state decides to put it, with tax structures and land. That means the map of where engineered biology is made is a map of industrial policy, not of scientific strength.

name: Shanghai Model Organisms Center
desc: WHAT. A Chinese supplier of genetically modified rodent models and custom model generation services, exporting internationally. WHERE IT SITS. The Asian pole of the transgenic animal trade, growing as costs push model generation eastward. WHY IT MATTERS. Model animals are increasingly made where it is cheapest and used where the research is published, under welfare law that applies at the point of creation rather than the point of use. A journal in one country publishes work on animals produced under another country's standard, and nothing in the paper records which.

name: Chinese assisted reproduction sector — NHC licensing
desc: WHAT. China's health commission, which licenses assisted reproduction clinics and prohibited germline editing after the 2018 gene-edited babies case. WHERE IT SITS. The largest national fertility sector by volume, under a licensing system tightened in direct response to a single researcher. WHY IT MATTERS. He Jiankui edited human embryos and served a prison sentence; China then wrote germline editing into its criminal law. It is the only jurisdiction where the prohibition arrived through prosecution rather than through anticipatory legislation, which is a different kind of deterrent and rests on a different kind of authority.

name: National Biosafety Board Malaysia
desc: WHAT. Malaysia's biosafety authority, publishing applications and decisions and running a public feedback period on each. WHERE IT SITS. A country whose palm oil sector makes it a target for engineered oil crops and for fermented substitutes at the same time. WHY IT MATTERS. Malaysia faces the industry from two directions: engineered palm improvement on one side, and precision-fermented oils designed to replace palm oil on the other. A producing country being offered both the upgrade and the replacement is a position the usual framing does not cover.

name: Ministerio del Ambiente — moratoria GMO
desc: WHAT. Peru's environment ministry, administering the national moratorium on the entry and production of GMOs, extended to 2035. WHERE IT SITS. Inside the centre of origin for potato, and one of the few long-running national moratoria anywhere. WHY IT MATTERS. Peru's moratorium is explicitly framed around protecting native agrobiodiversity rather than around safety, and it has been extended twice. It is the working example of a centre-of-origin argument carried into law and held there for over a decade.

name: AGES — Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety
desc: WHAT. Austria's food and seed safety agency, running systematic GM testing of seed lots and imported food and feed. WHERE IT SITS. The enforcement layer behind one of Europe's firmest GM-free positions. WHY IT MATTERS. Austria's position is enforceable rather than declaratory because the testing exists. A GM-free claim without a testing programme behind it is a statement of intent; with one, it is a fact that can be checked at the border. That distinction decides which national positions actually hold.

name: Ministry of the Environment — GMO register
desc: WHAT. Czechia's GMO authority, publishing the register of contained use, trials and cultivation. WHERE IT SITS. One of the few EU states that grew Bt maize commercially and then stopped, for market rather than legal reasons. WHY IT MATTERS. Czech farmers abandoned Bt maize because buyers and processors would not pay for it, not because it was prohibited. That is the market door this map keeps pointing at, working without any regulator involved.

name: Centro de Ingeniería Genética y Biotecnología
desc: WHAT. Cuba's state genetic engineering centre, which develops engineered crops, vaccines and biopharmaceuticals and holds the traits behind the country's GM maize and soy. WHERE IT SITS. A fully state-owned biotechnology sector with no private ownership layer at all. WHY IT MATTERS. Cuba is the clean test of whether the objections to this industry are objections to the technology or to who owns it. There is no patent-holding company, no royalty, no seed contract and no shareholder. The consent, containment and irreversibility questions remain exactly as they were; the ownership ones vanish. That separation is worth being able to see.

name: Comité Nacional de Bioseguridad
desc: WHAT. Bolivia's biosafety committee, operating under a constitution and a Law of Mother Earth that restrict GM crops, while GM soy is grown commercially in Santa Cruz. WHERE IT SITS. The widest gap on this map between what a country's law says and what is in its fields. WHY IT MATTERS. Bolivia has constitutional protection for native seed, a rights-of-nature statute, and roughly a million hectares of engineered soy. The law and the ground have been in open contradiction for years, which is worth knowing before treating any constitutional provision as decisive on its own.

name: Ministerio del Ambiente — bioseguridad
desc: WHAT. Ecuador's environment ministry, administering a constitutional declaration of the country as free of GM seeds and crops, with narrow research exceptions. WHERE IT SITS. One of only a handful of constitutional prohibitions in the world, alongside Mexico's maize amendment. WHY IT MATTERS. Ecuador wrote rights of nature into its constitution in 2008 and the GM prohibition alongside it. Enforcement has been contested and imports continue. A constitutional clause is harder to remove than a decree and no easier to enforce, which is the practical lesson for anyone pursuing that route.

name: Comisión Técnica Nacional de Bioseguridad
desc: WHAT. Costa Rica's biosafety commission, which authorises GM seed multiplication for export while most of its cantons have declared themselves GM-free. WHERE IT SITS. The same arrangement as Chile — seed grown for other countries' markets — but with organised local government refusal running against it. WHY IT MATTERS. A majority of Costa Rican cantons declared themselves GM-free through municipal votes while national authorisations continued. It is the clearest case anywhere of subnational refusal accumulating into a de facto national position without any national law changing.

name: National Environment Management Council
desc: WHAT. Tanzania's environmental authority, which administered a biosafety regime carrying strict liability and later suspended confined field trials outright. WHERE IT SITS. A country that adopted an unusually strict liability rule and then halted trials that had already been approved. WHY IT MATTERS. Strict liability means a developer carries the cost of harm without anyone having to prove negligence. Industry bodies campaigned against it explicitly as a barrier to investment, which is a clear statement of how much the absence of a liability rule is worth to them elsewhere.

name: National Biosafety Authority Zambia
desc: WHAT. Zambia's biosafety authority, in a country that refused GM food aid during the 2002 famine and has maintained a prohibition on GM cultivation since. WHERE IT SITS. The reference case for a state refusing engineered material under maximum pressure. WHY IT MATTERS. Zambia turned down food aid in a hunger crisis on the grounds that accepting grain would contaminate its seed stock and close its European export markets. It is cited by every side of this argument, for opposite reasons, and both readings rest on the same documented facts.

name: Ministry of Rural Development and Food
desc: WHAT. Greece's agriculture ministry, which exercised the EU opt-out to exclude its entire territory from GM cultivation under Directive (EU) 2015/412. WHERE IT SITS. Among the nineteen member states and regions that opted out territory-wide when the EU devolved cultivation decisions. WHY IT MATTERS. The opt-out mechanism was designed to break a deadlock by letting states refuse individually. Nineteen refused. A rule intended to enable cultivation by removing objections produced near-continental exclusion instead, which is worth knowing about how these mechanisms actually behave.

name: Ministry of Agriculture — GMO-free constitutional provision
desc: WHAT. Hungary's agriculture ministry, operating under a constitutional article committing the state to agriculture free of genetically modified organisms. WHERE IT SITS. The only EU member state with the prohibition written into its constitution. WHY IT MATTERS. Hungary destroyed hundreds of hectares of maize found to contain GM seed and publicised it. Whether that is enforcement or theatre, it demonstrates what a constitutional commitment produces in practice: the seed still arrived, and the response was destruction after the fact rather than prevention.

name: Office National de Sécurité Sanitaire des Produits Alimentaires
desc: WHAT. Morocco's food safety office, overseeing imports and the seed multiplication sector that supplies European vegetable breeders. WHERE IT SITS. Counter-season seed production for Europe, the North African counterpart to Chile's role for the Americas. WHY IT MATTERS. Seed multiplication moves to wherever labour and climate are cheapest, which puts a quiet and unexamined part of this industry in countries that have no commercial stake in the resulting varieties and often no register of what was grown.

name: Food and Drug Administration — GM food registration
desc: WHAT. Taiwan's regulator, running a mandatory GM food labelling regime and a public register of approved events. WHERE IT SITS. One of the stricter labelling regimes in Asia, in a large importer that grows no GM crops. WHY IT MATTERS. Taiwan prohibits GM ingredients in school meals by law. That is a rare thing: a rule that acts on a specific population rather than on the product, and it was carried by parents rather than by farmers, which is a different political base from most of this argument.

name: Saudi Food and Drug Authority — GM food rules
desc: WHAT. The regulator of one of the world's largest food-importing markets, operating a GM labelling requirement and an approved-event list. WHERE IT SITS. Import-side power without any domestic production to protect. WHY IT MATTERS. A large importer with no farm lobby has leverage that producing countries do not, and almost never uses it. What Gulf importers accept sets a de facto standard for the exporters selling to them, and those specifications are commercial documents rather than public policy.

name: International Rice Research Institute — Golden Rice
desc: WHAT. The programme behind vitamin-A-enriched rice, developed with public and philanthropic funding and approved in the Philippines before a court revoked the permits in 2024. WHERE IT SITS. The single most-argued-about engineered crop in the world, and the one always cited to show the technology can serve people rather than markets. WHY IT MATTERS. It is the strongest case the industry has and it took over two decades to reach a field, then lost its permits on monitoring grounds rather than on safety. Both facts are true at once: a genuinely public-interest product, and a demonstration that public-interest framing does not exempt a release from the procedural questions.

name: Norwegian Biotechnology Advisory Board
desc: WHAT. Norway's statutory advisory board on biotechnology, covering both agricultural and human applications, publishing its advice and its internal disagreements in English. WHERE IT SITS. One of very few bodies anywhere with a remit spanning crops, animals and human reproduction together. WHY IT MATTERS. Norway's Gene Technology Act requires that a product be judged on sustainability, societal benefit and ethics as well as safety — the only major framework that puts those in the statute rather than leaving them out of scope. Australia's regulator is barred from considering benefit at all. The contrast shows how much of what a regulator may think about is a drafting decision.

name: Rewriting Extinction / genetic biocontrol programmes
desc: WHAT. The research community developing genetic biocontrol for invasive species — engineered fish, rodents and insects intended to suppress introduced populations. WHERE IT SITS. Conservation as the application, with the same tools and the same irreversibility as agricultural release. WHY IT MATTERS. Genetic biocontrol scrambles the politics: the proponents are conservation biologists and the target is an invasive species most people would like gone. The consent question does not scramble with it. An island's rodents do not stay on the island, and neither do the genes.

name: Nature Conservancy — biotechnology in conservation
desc: WHAT. One of the world's largest conservation organisations, which has engaged formally with whether biotechnology should be used in conservation practice. WHERE IT SITS. The point at which the conservation sector has to decide whether it is a user of this industry or a check on it. WHY IT MATTERS. Large conservation organisations hold land, credibility and access to regulators. Whichever way they go on engineered releases will matter more than most national positions, and the internal argument is happening now with very little outside attention.

name: Wellcome Leap
desc: WHAT. A Wellcome-funded programme running large, fast, goal-directed research projects, including in cellular engineering and reproductive biology. WHERE IT SITS. Philanthropic money deliberately structured to move faster than grant cycles or public funders can. WHY IT MATTERS. Speed is the stated design goal. Whatever the merits, a funder built to outpace the deliberative machinery is also outpacing the ethical and regulatory review attached to it, and that is a structural feature rather than an oversight.

name: China National Seed Group (Syngenta / Sinochem)
desc: WHAT. China's largest seed company, inside the state-owned Sinochem structure alongside Syngenta. WHERE IT SITS. The consolidation of Chinese domestic seed into the same state group that owns a Western major. WHY IT MATTERS. One state holding company owns both a global agrochemical major and China's domestic seed champion. That is a concentration of a different kind from the Western four, answerable to a government rather than to shareholders, and no competition authority anywhere has jurisdiction over the combination.

name: European Bioinformatics Institute — model organism databases
desc: WHAT. The European infrastructure hosting the genome and variant databases underlying model organism research, including mouse, zebrafish and rat resources. WHERE IT SITS. The data layer beneath the animal trade — what makes a strain findable, comparable and reproducible. WHY IT MATTERS. These databases are the closest thing to an inventory of what has been engineered into a laboratory animal. No biosafety register comes near their completeness, and they exist for scientific rather than regulatory reasons, which is why they work.

name: USDA APHIS — annual research facility reports
desc: WHAT. The annual reports every registered US research facility must file, listing by species how many animals it used and how many were subjected to pain without relief, published as searchable data. WHERE IT SITS. The most complete public accounting of animal use anywhere, and still a partial one. WHY IT MATTERS. **Mice, rats and birds bred for research are excluded from the Animal Welfare Act's definition of an animal.** They are the overwhelming majority of animals used, and the great majority of genetically altered ones, so the figures in this report describe a small fraction of what happens and the rest is not counted anywhere by anyone.

name: Charles River — global site network
desc: WHAT. The site list for the largest research-animal supplier and preclinical contract laboratory in the world, spanning breeding facilities, testing laboratories and quarantine sites across the Americas, Europe and Asia. WHERE IT SITS. The single largest node in this facet, and both a breeder and a testing house. WHY IT MATTERS. Because the company publishes its own locations, this is the nearest thing to a map of the industry's physical footprint that exists. No regulator publishes an equivalent, in any country.

name: Jackson Laboratory — Bar Harbor
desc: WHAT. The breeding and distribution campus behind the world's reference collection of genetically defined mice, holding thousands of mutant and transgenic strains. WHERE IT SITS. Infrastructure rather than a supplier — a large share of published mouse research uses strains originating here. WHY IT MATTERS. Standardising the animal standardises the science. Thousands of strains exist because someone needed a specific disease phenotype bred into a living creature and kept alive as a line, and the catalogue is the clearest public statement of what that means at volume.

name: Wisconsin National Primate Research Center
desc: WHAT. One of the federally supported US primate centres, breeding and housing macaques and marmosets for research including genetic modification. WHERE IT SITS. Among the largest primate colonies in the country, publicly funded. WHY IT MATTERS. Primate supply is a chronic constraint, and the shortage drives both domestic breeding expansion and an international trade that has produced smuggling prosecutions. The scarcity is what makes that trade lucrative and the enforcement problems predictable.

name: Inotiv — facility network
desc: WHAT. The site list for the supplier and preclinical services company that absorbed Envigo's animal business, covering breeding and testing facilities across the United States and Europe. WHERE IT SITS. Second only to Charles River in research-animal supply. WHY IT MATTERS. Its predecessor's Cumberland beagle facility was closed after a federal enforcement action, and roughly four thousand dogs were removed and rehomed. Consolidation means welfare standards across an entire research sector rest on very few companies, and an action against one has consequences at that scale.

name: Home Office — licensed establishments
desc: WHAT. The licensing regime under the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act, requiring a licence for the establishment, the project and the individual, with annual statistics by species, severity and purpose. WHERE IT SITS. The most detailed national accounting in the world, and the only one that separately counts animals bred and killed to maintain genetically altered lines. WHY IT MATTERS. That separate count is the point. A large share of licensed procedures are not experiments at all — they are the creation and upkeep of engineered lines. Nowhere else publishes that number, so nowhere else can say what the model-organism trade actually costs.

name: The Francis Crick Institute — animal research
desc: WHAT. One of Europe's largest biomedical research institutes, publishing its animal numbers, species and the reasoning behind their use. WHERE IT SITS. A single very large facility inside a national system that requires disclosure. WHY IT MATTERS. Institutional openness of this kind exists because the law and a sector concordat require it, not because institutes chose it. Where neither applies, the same work happens and no figure is published.

name: German Primate Center (DPZ)
desc: WHAT. Germany's national primate research institute, breeding and housing macaques and marmosets and running neuroscience and infection research. WHERE IT SITS. The largest primate research facility in Germany, publicly funded. WHY IT MATTERS. Primate work is where the ethical argument is sharpest and the alternatives thinnest, and it is concentrated in a handful of national institutes. Naming them is most of what public scrutiny of this facet can consist of.

name: Biomedical Primate Research Centre
desc: WHAT. Europe's largest primate research centre, in Rijswijk, breeding macaques and marmosets for infectious disease and neuroscience research. WHERE IT SITS. The continental counterpart to the US primate centres. WHY IT MATTERS. The Dutch parliament has repeatedly debated winding it down, and it continues. A facility surviving explicit political pressure to close is a better measure of how entrenched this work is than any statistic about it.

name: Charles River / Janvier — European breeding sites
desc: WHAT. The site list for the largest European breeder of laboratory rodents, including genetically modified strains. WHERE IT SITS. The European supply line — animals do not travel well, so each region breeds its own. WHY IT MATTERS. Welfare law applies where an animal is bred and used. The research travels everywhere, so results generated under one standard enter a shared evidence base without the standard travelling with them, and nothing in a published paper records which applied.

name: Guangdong / Hainan primate breeding sector
desc: WHAT. The Chinese non-human primate breeding industry, which supplies a large share of the world's research macaques, concentrated in southern provinces. WHERE IT SITS. The origin of most of the global primate supply, and the chokepoint that became visible when exports were suspended in 2020. WHY IT MATTERS. When that supply stopped, prices rose several-fold and Western research programmes stalled, which demonstrated how completely the rest of the world depends on breeding capacity in one country. It is the clearest dependency in this facet and it is almost never discussed as one.

name: Cyagen — Suzhou and Santa Clara facilities
desc: WHAT. Custom transgenic and knockout animal model generation, with breeding and cryopreservation facilities in China and the United States. WHERE IT SITS. Made-to-order animal engineering, sold as a catalogue service with a lead time. WHY IT MATTERS. A researcher can commission an animal that does not yet exist, to a written specification, and receive it as a product. Contained use rarely generates a public entry, so the largest volume of vertebrate engineering in the world is also the least recorded.

name: RIKEN BioResource Research Center
desc: WHAT. Japan's national bioresource centre, distributing genetically engineered mouse strains, cell lines and other research materials internationally. WHERE IT SITS. The Asian counterpart to Jackson and the European mouse repositories. WHY IT MATTERS. Public repositories are the most complete inventory of what has been engineered into a mammal that exists. They are far more thorough than any biosafety register, and they were built for scientific reasons rather than regulatory ones — which is why they work.

name: Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals
desc: WHAT. India's statutory body registering and inspecting animal research establishments and approving protocols. WHERE IT SITS. The oversight layer for a rapidly growing contract research sector doing preclinical work for clients elsewhere. WHY IT MATTERS. A very large share of the world's preclinical animal work now happens in India and China. The regulator reading the resulting study is usually in a third country, applying its own standards to work it did not observe, under welfare law that does not reach the place the work was done.

name: European Commission — ALURES animal use database
desc: WHAT. The EU's statistical database of animal use under Directive 2010/63/EU, reporting by species, purpose, severity and genetic status across member states. WHERE IT SITS. The only multi-country dataset on this subject in existence. WHY IT MATTERS. It reports the creation and maintenance of genetically altered lines separately from experimental use, as the UK does, and covers 27 countries. It is also the outer limit of what is known: outside the EU, the UK and the partial US count, there is no systematic reporting of animal use anywhere, and the global total is genuinely unknown.

name: Arnold & Porter — agricultural biotechnology practice
desc: WHAT. A Washington firm with a long-standing food, drug and agriculture regulatory practice, representing developers through APHIS, EPA and FDA review. WHERE IT SITS. Between the applicant and the regulator, drafting the submissions the agency reads. WHY IT MATTERS. Regulatory law firms shape what a dossier contains and what it leaves out, and they carry knowledge of an agency's habits across dozens of applications. There is no equivalent capability on the objector's side, in any country, and that asymmetry decides more outcomes than the science in any single file.

name: Covington & Burling — food and drug regulatory
desc: WHAT. One of the largest regulatory practices in Washington, advising life-sciences and agricultural clients on approvals, labelling and enforcement. WHERE IT SITS. The revolving door's hinge — firms of this kind employ former agency officials and return staff to agencies. WHY IT MATTERS. Committee memberships and previous employers are public and checkable, and an hour spent on them is often the most quoted thing a small group produces. The point is not wrongdoing; it is that the people writing the submissions and the people reading them come from the same small professional world.

name: US Patent and Trademark Office — patent full-text search
desc: WHAT. The searchable full text of granted US patents and applications, including claims over engineered plants, animals, methods and gene sequences. WHERE IT SITS. Where ownership of living material is actually granted, and where it can be read. WHY IT MATTERS. The claims are the property, not the abstract. A patent that names a specific construct and one that reaches any plant containing a gene variant look similar on the front page and mean entirely different things, and only the numbered claims at the end say which it is.

name: Patent Trial and Appeal Board
desc: WHAT. The tribunal that hears challenges to granted US patents, including the CRISPR interference proceedings between the Broad Institute and the Berkeley group. WHERE IT SITS. Where the foundational ownership of gene editing was actually decided — not in a laboratory and not in Congress. WHY IT MATTERS. The record is public and it is the clearest available account of how a publicly funded technique became private property, written by the parties themselves under oath.

name: Bayer Crop Science — divisional leadership
desc: WHAT. The published leadership of the largest seed and agricultural-trait business in the world, with each executive's remit. WHERE IT SITS. Where decisions affecting several hundred million hectares are actually taken, by a small number of named people. WHY IT MATTERS. Companies are argued with as if they were weather. They are not: a division has a head, that person has a public name and a stated remit, and correspondence addressed to a named executive is answered differently from correspondence addressed to a company. The leadership page is the starting point almost nobody uses.

name: Broad Institute — CRISPR inventors and the patent record
desc: WHAT. The institute's own account of the CRISPR work of Feng Zhang and colleagues, and of the patent estate built on it. WHERE IT SITS. One side of the foundational ownership dispute; the Doudna–Charpentier work at Berkeley and Vienna is the other. WHY IT MATTERS. Both groups did publicly funded research, both won Nobel recognition or its equivalent for it, and the commercial rights ended up licensed exclusively in agriculture. The individuals are not the problem; the arrangement that converts their work into an exclusive licence is, and it operated the same way regardless of who won.

name: Innovative Genomics Institute — Jennifer Doudna
desc: WHAT. The Berkeley institute founded by Jennifer Doudna, running CRISPR research and an explicit programme on access and affordability of genome-editing medicine. WHERE IT SITS. The other side of the patent dispute, and an unusual case: a founder of the technique publicly arguing that its medicines are priced beyond the people who need them. WHY IT MATTERS. The strongest critique of gene therapy pricing comes from inside the field rather than outside it. That is worth knowing before treating the industry as monolithic, and worth citing because it cannot be dismissed as scientific illiteracy.

name: Colossal Biosciences — founders and scientific advisers
desc: WHAT. The published team and advisory board of the best-funded de-extinction venture, including George Church, whose laboratory has seeded a long list of biotechnology companies. WHERE IT SITS. Where academic credibility is attached to a venture-funded project, which is what makes it fundable and reportable. WHY IT MATTERS. Advisory boards transfer reputation. A named scientist on a company's board is doing work for that company whether or not they are paid, and the arrangement is disclosed on the company's own site — which makes it checkable rather than alleged.

name: European Patent Office — opposition register
desc: WHAT. The register of European patents and of oppositions filed against them, with every submission and decision published. WHERE IT SITS. The nine-month window after grant in which **any person** may oppose a European patent, with no standing requirement and no lawyer needed to file. WHY IT MATTERS. Patents last twenty years and apply across the whole region at once, and polling across several European countries has found large majorities opposed to patents on seeds. It is the widest gap on this map between how much public support a position has and how few people act on it.

name: No Patents on Seeds
desc: WHAT. The coalition that has run patent oppositions on plants and animals at the European Patent Office for over a decade, publishing the patents it finds and the outcomes. WHERE IT SITS. Effectively the only organised use of the opposition procedure against this industry. WHY IT MATTERS. It documents patents claiming naturally occurring gene variants, which extend to plants bred conventionally and so work around the prohibition on patenting essentially biological processes. The cost falls hardest on small breeders, who abandon projects rather than risk infringement they cannot afford to defend.

name: EU Transparency Register — biotechnology lobbying
desc: WHAT. The register of organisations lobbying the EU institutions, with declared annual spend, staff numbers and the files each is working on. WHERE IT SITS. The one place the industry's political spending is stated by the industry itself. WHY IT MATTERS. Declared figures run to millions per firm per year, plus trade association fees on top. The numbers are self-declared and therefore a floor rather than a measure, which is worth saying whenever they are quoted — including here.

name: Euroseeds
desc: WHAT. The European seed sector's trade association, representing breeders and seed companies on plant variety rights, new genomic techniques and seed marketing law. WHERE IT SITS. Alongside CropLife in Brussels, working the same institutions on the adjacent file. WHY IT MATTERS. Seed marketing law decides what may legally be sold and therefore what farmers can buy, and it is argued over almost entirely by the sector it governs. Very few objectors appear at the committee stage where these bills are settled.

name: He Jiankui — the germline case and its aftermath
desc: WHAT. The researcher who announced in 2018 that he had edited the genomes of human embryos that were brought to term, was convicted of illegal medical practice in China and imprisoned for three years, and has since resumed publicly announcing embryo research. WHERE IT SITS. The only completed case of heritable human genome editing, and the event that produced China's criminal prohibition. WHY IT MATTERS. The scientific community's response was a moratorium with no legal force, issued by people who were not the ones proceeding. What actually stopped it was a criminal prosecution. That distinction matters for every part of this map where self-governance is offered as sufficient.

name: Rothamsted Research
desc: WHAT. One of the world's oldest agricultural research stations, running publicly funded GM and gene-edited field trials including omega-3 camelina and modified wheat. WHERE IT SITS. Public-sector field trials, which face the same objections as corporate ones and answer to a different constituency. WHY IT MATTERS. Its trials have been the focus of protest and of court proceedings, and it publishes its applications and results. A public institute is the case where the ownership objection falls away and the containment and consent objections remain — which is a useful test of which argument someone is actually making.

name: Syngenta — sustainability and regulatory reporting
desc: WHAT. The company's own reporting on pesticide sales, product stewardship and regulatory status across markets. WHERE IT SITS. The self-account of the largest pesticide business in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. Reporting of this kind is where a company states which of its products are restricted in which markets, which is a fact it would rather not assemble but must. Reading it alongside the sales figures shows how much revenue comes from products a country has already decided against.

name: OECD — Working Party on Biotechnology
desc: WHAT. The intergovernmental body that develops consensus documents on the safety assessment of engineered organisms, and that maintains the unique identifier system. WHERE IT SITS. Above national regulators, setting the technical vocabulary they all use. WHY IT MATTERS. Consensus documents are drafted by delegations that include national regulators and, in practice, industry input. They are not binding and they are followed anyway, which makes this one of the least examined and most consequential rooms in the whole structure.

name: FAO — biotechnology and biosafety
desc: WHAT. The UN food agency's programme on agricultural biotechnology, including capacity-building for national biosafety systems in low-income countries. WHERE IT SITS. Where national regulatory frameworks in much of the world are actually designed, with donor funding. WHY IT MATTERS. A biosafety framework built with external technical assistance tends to resemble the frameworks of whoever provided it. That is how regulatory approaches spread, and it happens well before any product application appears.
